params.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with three weeks of daily spiking fevers, a salmon-pink rash that appears with each fever spike and fades in between, and arthritis of both wrists. Which JIA subtype fits this presentation, and what is its most dangerous complication?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oligoarticular JIA affects four or fewer joints, typically in young girls, without systemic features like daily spiking fevers or an evanescent rash. Uveitis is its major extra-articular risk, but this child's prominent systemic features point to a different subtype.
RF-positive polyarticular JIA presents with symmetric small-joint arthritis in older children, resembling adult rheumatoid arthritis. It does not cause daily spiking fevers or a salmon-pink rash.

Correct — daily spiking fevers, a fleeting salmon-pink rash that comes and goes with fever spikes, and arthritis are the hallmarks of systemic JIA. Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is its most dangerous complication — a life-threatening over-activation of the immune system that requires urgent recognition.
Enthesitis-related arthritis typically affects older boys with enthesitis at tendon insertion sites and HLA-B27 positivity. It does not present with spiking fevers and an evanescent rash.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinguishing features: daily spiking fevers with a salmon-pink rash that appears and disappears with each spike are the signature of systemic JIA, not the other subtypes.
Well done. The triad of quotidian fever, evanescent salmon-pink rash, and arthritis is the signature of systemic JIA — and MAS is the complication you must never miss.

interactions.label: What distinguishes the purpura of Henoch-Schönlein purpura from the petechiae se

params.question: What distinguishes the purpura of Henoch-Schönlein purpura from the petechiae seen in thrombocytopenic conditions?

answers.text: HSP purpura appears predominantly on the face and upper limbs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HSP purpura characteristically appears symmetrically on the buttocks and lower limbs, not the face or upper limbs. This gravity-dependent distribution is a clinical clue.

answers.text: HSP purpura is flat and blanches on pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HSP purpura is raised (palpable), not flat, and does NOT blanch on pressure. The raised nature results from inflammatory cell infiltration of the small vessel walls, causing them to leak.

answers.text: HSP purpura is palpable (raised) due to vasculitic inflammation, and the platelet count remains normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — palpable purpura is the hallmark of HSP. Inflamed small vessels leak blood and become infiltrated by inflammatory cells, producing raised lesions you can feel above the skin surface. The platelet count stays normal because this is vasculitic bleeding, not a clotting deficiency.

answers.text: HSP purpura is always preceded by a gastrointestinal infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HSP typically follows an upper respiratory tract infection, not a gastrointestinal infection. The rash usually appears one to three weeks after the URTI.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: HSP purpura is raised (palpable) because inflamed vessels leak and get infiltrated by inflammatory cells, and the platelet count remains normal. This distinguishes it from thrombocytopenic conditions.
Exactly right. Palpable purpura with a normal platelet count is the defining clue — vasculitic bleeding, not a clotting problem.

params.question: The malar (butterfly) rash of SLE involves the nasolabial folds, which helps distinguish it from the sparing pattern seen in rosacea.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement reverses the actual pattern. The malar rash of SLE SPARES the nasolabial folds, while rosacea INVOLVES them. Remembering this sparing pattern is essential for distinguishing lupus from other facial rashes.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement reverses the actual pattern. The malar rash of SLE characteristically SPARES the nasolabial folds, while rosacea INVOLVES them. This sparing is a key clinical clue for recognising lupus early.

params.question: A child has had a warm, swollen knee for three weeks after a viral illness. He has stopped running but does not complain of pain. Why is it too early to diagnose juvenile idiopathic arthritis?

answers.text: Autoantibodies need six weeks to become detectable in blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ANA and other autoantibodies may be present at any point during the disease course. The six-week criterion is not based on antibody detection kinetics.

answers.text: Joint erosion requires six weeks to become visible on X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Joint damage on X-ray is a late finding in JIA, occurring after months to years of inflammation. The six-week rule has nothing to do with radiological changes.

answers.text: The six-week threshold exists to exclude transient reactive arthritis, which typically resolves within this period

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — reactive arthritis following viral infections commonly resolves within six weeks. The six-week threshold is a deliberate diagnostic criterion that prevents labelling a self-limiting condition as a chronic disease like JIA.

answers.text: JIA can only be diagnosed after a rheumatoid factor test has been repeated twice, four weeks apart

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rheumatoid factor is negative in most JIA subtypes and its testing schedule does not determine the diagnostic timeline. The six-week criterion is based on clinical duration of arthritis, not laboratory repetition.

overallFeedback.feedback: The six-week criterion exists because reactive arthritis — the most common mimic — typically resolves before six weeks. Only when arthritis persists beyond this threshold does a chronic diagnosis like JIA become appropriate.
Exactly. The six-week cutoff is a clinical safeguard — it prevents overdiagnosing transient post-viral arthritis as a chronic condition.

interactions.label: A 5-year-old girl with oligoarticular JIA has a positive ANA at 1:320. Her eyes

params.question: A 5-year-old girl with oligoarticular JIA has a positive ANA at 1:320. Her eyes appear completely normal on external examination. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Reassure the parents that the eye risk is low since both eyes look normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic anterior uveitis in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA is often a 'white eye' — externally normal while active inflammation damages internal structures. A normal external appearance does NOT rule out uveitis.

answers.text: Order anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies to evaluate for lupus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While anti-dsDNA is useful when lupus is suspected, the immediate clinical priority in an ANA-positive child with oligoarticular JIA is uveitis screening, since delayed detection leads to irreversible vision loss.

answers.text: Arrange slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist, to be repeated every three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct — ANA positivity at ≥1:160 in a young child with oligoarticular JIA is the strongest predictor of chronic anterior uveitis. This inflammation is clinically silent, so slit-lamp screening every three months is mandatory, particularly in children under six, regardless of whether the eyes look normal.
Prophylactic topical steroids are not indicated. The correct approach is regular slit-lamp screening to detect uveitis early, followed by targeted treatment only if inflammation is found.

overallFeedback.feedback: A positive ANA in oligoarticular JIA is the strongest predictor of chronic anterior uveitis, which is often clinically silent. Slit-lamp examination every three months is the mandatory next step, regardless of how the eyes look.
Well done. The take-home message: a positive ANA in oligoarticular JIA means mandatory slit-lamp screening — never rely on the external eye appearance.
